title: What is a Decision Tree?
description: How decision trees split data recursively using impurity measures - entropy, Gini impurity and information gain - for classification and regression.
content:
**Decision tree** is a machine learning algorithm used for both classification and regression tasks. It is a hierarchical model consisting of:
• Nodes
• Branches
• Leaves

Each internal node represents a decision based on the input, each branch represents the outcome of that decision, and each leaf represents the final decision or prediction.

Decision trees work recursively by partitioning the feature space into smaller subsets based on significant features. The selection of a split is made by evaluating various splitting criteria - common ones are measures based on impurity, such as entropy or the Gini coefficient. This process continues until a stopping criterion is met.

Decision trees actually rely on measures of impurity - two common metrics are entropy and Gini impurity. By comparing impurity before and after a split, the algorithm computes the information gain.

**Entropy** measures the uncertainty or disorder of the data. For classification, the entropy at a node is calculated as the negative sum of p(i) · log₂ p(i), where p(i) is the proportion of examples of class i among N possible classes. Nodes with only one class (i.e., completely pure) have an entropy of 0.

**Gini impurity** estimates the probability of misclassification when randomly choosing an element from the node and labeling it. It is defined as 1 − Σ p(i)².

**Information gain** is the reduction of impurity due to a split. It is computed as the difference between the impurity of the parent node and the weighted sum of the impurities of the children nodes. A high information gain indicates that the split has effectively separated the data into distinct classes.
